Testator
tes-tā'tor
n. (one who makes a testament or will; in Hebrews, the one whose death gives the covenant its force)
Latin testator, from testari, to bear witness, to make a will. The Greek behind it in Hebrews 9 is diatithemai, the participle of the verb from which diatheke — covenant, testament — is formed.

Biblical Definition

“For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator” (Hebrews 9:16). The writer is pressing a point the whole epistle exists to make: the new covenant is in force because Christ died. The Greek word diatheke carries both senses — a covenant God cuts with men, and a testament that disposes an inheritance — and Hebrews 9 works the second sense deliberately. A will is a dead letter while the man who wrote it lives; his heirs have a promise and nothing in hand. “For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth” (Hebrews 9:17). So the inheritance named in the everlasting covenant waited on a death, and the death was the Testator's own. “And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance” (Hebrews 9:15). This is why the blood is not incidental. “Without shedding of blood is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22) is not a ritual preference but the law of the testament: the heirs inherit because the Testator died, and He lives again to execute His own will.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a testator as a man who makes and leaves a will or testament at death.

expand to see more

TESTATOR, n. A man who makes and leaves a will or testament at death.

TESTAMENT, n. A solemn authentic instrument in writing, by which a person declares his will as to the disposal of his estate and effects after his death.

2. The name of each general division of the canonical books of the sacred Scriptures; as the Old Testament; the New Testament.

INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession.

MEDIATOR, n. One that interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 9:16 — "For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator."

Hebrews 9:17 — "For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth."

Hebrews 9:15 — "And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance."

Hebrews 9:22 — "And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission."

Modern Corruption

The death of the Testator is treated as a moving example rather than the legal instrument that conveys the inheritance.

expand to see more

Modern preaching regularly reduces the cross to a demonstration — God showing how much He loves us, Christ modelling self-giving. Hebrews 9 will not permit it. A testament is a legal instrument, and the writer's whole argument turns on a point of law: the will does not operate until the testator dies. An example changes nothing about an estate. Only a death transfers it. The moral-influence theory of the atonement, revived by Abelard and made respectable again by nineteenth-century liberalism, empties this chapter of its argument, because an influence conveys no inheritance and remits no transgression.

The second error runs through the sacramental systems that must repeat the death because they cannot rest in it. The Roman mass re-presents the sacrifice at every altar; Hebrews answers that Christ was “once offered to bear the sins of many,” and that a testament executed once needs no re-execution. Here the figure is exact and decisive: no man reads his father's will a second time to make the estate transfer again. The Testator died, the will is in force, and the heirs' part is to receive what has already been conveyed to them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diatheke (G1242), covenant or testament — Hebrews 9:15-17; the participle diathemenos (G1303) is the testator himself.

expand to see more

Greek diatheke (G1242) — covenant, testament; 33 occurrences, and Hebrews 9 turns on its double sense.

Greek diatithemai (G1303) — to appoint, to make a will; its participle is the testator of Hebrews 9:16-17.

Greek kleronomia (G2817) — inheritance; Hebrews 9:15, the eternal inheritance the testament conveys.

Greek mesites (G3316) — mediator; Hebrews 9:15, 1 Timothy 2:5 — one Mediator, and He is the Testator too.

Hebrews 9:22 gives the law of the instrument: without shedding of blood is no remission.

Usage

"“There must also of necessity be the death of the testator” — the cross as legal instrument, not illustration."

"“Of no strength at all while the testator liveth” — the inheritance waited on a death."

"The Testator died and rose; He executes His own will."
